title: Max Value of Equation
statement: Each entry of `points` is a point `[x, y]` of the plane, and the entries are ordered so that their x-coordinates strictly increase. A pair of entries `i < j` qualifies when its x-coordinates are at most `k` apart, that is `|x_i - x_j| <= k`, and its score is `y_i + y_j + |x_i - x_j|`. Return the highest score of any qualifying pair. The input always contains at least one qualifying pair.
constraints: x_i < x_j for all i < j (x strictly increases)
At least one pair has |x_i - x_j| <= k
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every pair is O(n²). Because x strictly increases, for `i < j` the score is `y_i + y_j + x_j - x_i = (y_i - x_i) + (x_j + y_j)`. So when point `j` is reached, it needs the largest `y_i - x_i` among earlier points whose x is within `k` of `x_j`. That is a sliding-window maximum, which a monotonic deque answers in O(1) amortized time per point.

## Approach

1. Keep `deque` of earlier points as `[x, gain]` with `gain = y - x`, gains strictly decreasing from front (`head`) to back.
2. For each point `[x, y]`, drop front entries whose x is more than `k` behind: they are out of range now and for every later point.
3. If anything remains, the front has the largest `gain` in range, so update `best` with `deque[head][1] + x + y`.
4. Pop back entries whose `gain` is at most the new point's `gain`: the new point is both better and stays in range longer, so they can never win.
5. Push the new point and continue; return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`points = [[1,3],[2,0],[5,10],[6,-10]]`, `k = 1`.

- `[1,3]`: deque empty; push `[1, 2]`.
- `[2,0]`: `2 - 1 <= 1`, so front stays; `best = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4`. Its gain `-2` is smaller, so push `[2, -2]`.
- `[5,10]`: both entries are more than 1 behind and leave; push `[5, 5]`.
- `[6,-10]`: front `[5, 5]` is in range; `5 + 6 - 10 = 1 < 4`. Push `[6, -16]`.

The answer is `4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): every point enters the deque once and leaves at most once.
- Space: O(n) for the deque in the worst case.

## Pitfalls

- Expire from the front by distance (`x - deque[head][0] > k`) **before** reading the maximum, or a pair farther than `k` apart is counted.
- Read the front **before** pushing the current point, so a point is never paired with itself.
- Start `best` at `-Infinity`, not 0: every qualifying score can be negative.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `deque` | earlier points `[x, gain]` that can still win, gains decreasing |
| `head` | index of the deque's front in the array |
| `best` | highest score found so far |
| `x`, `y` | coordinates of the current point |
| `gain` | `y - x`, what the current point adds when it is the left point |

narration.2: The deque keeps earlier points as [x, y - x], with y - x decreasing from front to back.
narration.3: head marks the front of the deque; entries before it have been dropped.
narration.4: Scores can be negative, so start below any possible value.
narration.6: Treat each point in turn as the right point of a pair.
narration.7: The front point is too far to the left to pair with this or any later point...
narration.10: Some earlier point is within k.
narration.11: The front has the largest y - x in range; adding x + y gives the best score ending here.
narration.13: This point's value when it later serves as the left point of a pair.
narration.14: Back entries with no larger y - x than this point can never beat it, since it also stays in range longer.
narration.17: Add this point as a candidate left point for later points.
narration.19: The largest score seen over all right points is the answer.
